extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research papers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty), authors preparing LaTeX manuscripts and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical stylistic and substantive guidelines for writing mathematical research papers and proofs, covering logical justification, exposition, LaTeX practices, and nitpicks of usage and punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify each step
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim does not follow immediately from the previous sentence alone, explain what it does follow from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Combining the previous two sentences shows that...' or 'By Lemma 8.3, ...'. Ensure every logical step is made explicit enough for the reader to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach reasons to each claim in multi-claim sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences that make multiple claims, attach reasons to each claim so the logic is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place reasons before/after the chain of claims or use a display (e.g. \begin{align*}) with right-hand justifications to associate explanations to individual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-sentence understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader at the period should know why each claim is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proof or justification comes later, explicitly signal this (for example, '..., as we now explain'). Do not leave the reader wondering at sentence end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Your wording must not admit any interpretation other than the intended one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's insufficient that words can be interpreted correctly; rewrite to remove alternate readings and ambiguous scope (quantifiers, modifiers, antecedents, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long arguments into lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose long arguments into lemmas even if they are used only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces cognitive load by minimising what the reader must keep in mind and clarifies logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate which results will be needed later and which are incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one of several propositions is needed later, say so explicitly to guide the reader's attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers must be unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Write quantifiers explicitly (e.g., 'for all x ∈ R' or 'for some x ∈ R') rather than leaving them implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bare 'for x ∈ R' constructions where the intended quantifier is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate where each hypothesis is used
rubrics_metrics.description: In proofs, state where and how each hypothesis of a theorem or lemma is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps readers verify necessity and understand dependencies among assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations specify location
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing, specify theorem number or page if referencing part of a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only omit location when citing the entire work; otherwise point the reader to the exact place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite published versions over preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer citing published versions of work rather than preprints when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published references are more stable and authoritative; use preprints only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv preprints: include version/date
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing arXiv preprints, include the version number or precise date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This removes ambiguity about which draft is being referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Forthcoming work' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Forthcoming work' should be used only if a publicly available preprint exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't cite something as forthcoming without a way for readers to access it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matryoshka rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Title, abstract, introduction, and body should each describe the entire article, with progressively more detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each level is a compressed summary of the next; the title is most compressed, the body the most detailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title length
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles should be long enough to convey content and specific enough to distinguish the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid titles that are too vague or too short to indicate topic and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'A note on', 'Remarks on' in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use phrases like 'A note on' or 'Remarks on' in titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such prefixes weaken the title; state the content directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract states main results
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should state the main results when they fit; omit detailed precision-only definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the primary contributions clear up front in the abstract rather than deferring to the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract is self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must be self-contained: do not include citations or references to the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should understand the abstract without consulting the paper; avoid 'see Section X' or 'as above'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get to new theorems fast in the introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: State your new theorems early in the introduction; postponing notation to a later section is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers want to see what is new quickly; provide informal statements if necessary and defer technical setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math papers usually do not have conclusions sections
rubrics_metrics.description: It is uncommon for math papers to include a separate conclusions section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, summarize contributions in the introduction or remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem statements short; definitions precede theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep theorem statements concise and put necessary definitions before the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burdening theorem statements with technical set-up that should be defined first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences short
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer short sentences and combine only when combining clarifies logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sentences help readability; long convoluted sentences obscure argument structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain equalities in correct order
rubrics_metrics.description: Write chained equalities in the correct logical order; remember transitivity applies universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful that each step in a chain is valid and written in a readable sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easier parts first in multi-part proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof has several parts, present the easier parts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This order aids comprehension and builds toward harder pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism claims: specify the map
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming two objects are isomorphic, specify the isomorphism explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming or describing the map prevents ambiguity and makes the claim verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction: choose base case for simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Start induction at n=0 if that is easier than starting at n=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the base case to make the induction straightforward and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Clear' is suspicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'clear' as an explanation; often it hides an omitted argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something is labeled 'clear', provide an explanation—readers may require the omitted detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce definitions and variables before they appear; avoid ', where ...' constructions that introduce symbols after use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variables should be introduced prior to reference to prevent confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence subjects can't span formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sentence subjects that are interrupted by displayed or inline formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences so the grammatical subject is not broken by formula notation (e.g., keep 'the discriminant ∆' as a continuous phrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skip filler intros
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases like 'We now prove the following proposition' which add nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin directly with the proposition or proof content to keep prose concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: No abbreviations in formal text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid abbreviations like 'WLOG', 'iff', 's.t.' in formal writing (they may be acceptable on blackboards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out phrases ('without loss of generality', 'if and only if', 'such that') in written work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write quantifiers in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words for quantifiers: write 'there exists' and 'for all' instead of ∃, ∀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves readability for general audiences and prevents overuse of symbols in sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with a mathematical symbol; make a grammatical subject first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a bad sentence: 'H denotes the Sylow p-subgroup' as a full sentence starting with symbol—rephrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: No contractions in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions such as 'don't' in formal mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full forms ('do not') to maintain a formal tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proof over contradiction when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use proof-by-contradiction when a direct proof suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct proofs are usually clearer; reserve contradiction for when direct approaches are awkward or unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to theorems by number
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a specific prior result, refer to it by its number rather than 'the previous theorem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered references are unambiguous even if the document structure changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single numbering for all theorem-like environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single numbering sequence for theorems, lemmas, propositions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent numbering simplifies cross-references and reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \DeclareMathOperator for operator names
rubrics_metrics.description: Define operator-style names with \DeclareMathOperator in LaTeX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces correct spacing and formatting for named operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: \hfill before \begin{enumerate} to prevent misalignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert \hfill before \begin{enumerate} to avoid first-item misalignment in certain layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A TeX/LaTeX nitpick to improve visual alignment of enumerated lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \colon for function maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Write f \colon X \to Y rather than f : X \to Y to get correct math spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proper LaTeX spacing commands to make maps and punctuation look correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using \usepackage{fullpage}, \usepackage{microtype}, \usepackage{colonequals}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These packages improve page layout, typographic quality, and colon-in-definition formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: "so that" vs "such that"
rubrics_metrics.description: "So that" implies purpose; "such that" imposes a condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace by 'in order that' / 'with the result that' if the meaning is purposive; choose carefully based on intended semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: "so" for plain implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'so' to indicate plain implication (e.g., 'A, so B').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that mirrors logical flow; 'so' signals consequence rather than purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect sentences with comma + conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer comma + conjunction to connect sentences; avoid bare semicolons unless a colon explains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punctuation to reflect grammatical and logical relations between clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only' must go next to the word it modifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplacing 'only' changes meaning; place it directly before or after its intended target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase 'Given an element g of G'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'Given an element g of G' rather than 'Given g an element of G.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural English order to introduce elements to avoid awkward constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Let,' the variable being defined
rubrics_metrics.description: After 'Let,' immediately state the variable being defined (e.g., 'Let Z be the center of G').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'Let the center of G be Z' when it obscures which object is being introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Theorem' when referring by number
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Theorem' when referring to a numbered theorem (e.g., 'Theorem 2.1').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows standard typographic convention for named numbered items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display formulas retain prior punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure display formulas keep the punctuation that preceded them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sentence ends with a displayed equation, include the appropriate punctuation before the display as part of the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Assume that G is a finite group' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'Assume that G is a finite group' over 'Assume G is a finite group' unless the latter appears inside a noun phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full clause forms to avoid informal ellipsis in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decade formatting: 'the 1980s'
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'the 1980s' rather than 'the 1980's'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using an apostrophe for plural decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: i.e./e.g. comma usage
rubrics_metrics.description: In American English, place a comma after 'i.e.' and 'e.g.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow American punctuation conventions for these abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer notational forms that reduce parentheses: write 'log x' instead of 'log(x)'; 'sin 2x' is fine; use parens for 'sin(x+y)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use parentheses when they clarify grouping or avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skip multiplication symbols when unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit multiplication symbols where juxtaposition is unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use juxtaposition (ab) rather than a ⋅ or × when context permits readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'We remark that' is filler
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting remarks with 'We remark that' unless the alternative begins with a symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase is often filler—lead with the substantive remark directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 'This concludes the proof' with QED
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write 'This concludes the proof' if you include a QED symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The QED symbol suffices to indicate the proof's end; extra phrase is redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions in exponents/subscripts use slash
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a slash for fractions in exponents/subscripts rather than stacked fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use x^{1/2} rather than x^{\frac{1}{2}} for inline clarity; avoid tall stacked fractions in superscripts/subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences are tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: Denote sequences as tuples: '(a_i)_{i≥0}' rather than set notation '{a_i}_{i≥0}'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tuple notation clarifies ordering and indexing; set notation can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Principal" vs "principle"
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Principal' means main; 'principle' means rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct word choice to avoid semantic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell-check common pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for commonly misspelled mathematical terms: 'separable' (not 'seperable'), 'archimedean' (not 'archimedian'), 'homogeneous' (not 'homogenous').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run spell-check with domain-aware corrections when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hyphen in 'non-' prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hyphenate 'non-' prefixes: use 'nonempty', 'nonzero', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard mathematical typography for prefixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals for most numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals for most numbers except single-digit counting numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventional rules about when to spell out numbers versus using digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'since' preferred over 'as'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'since' rather than 'as' to avoid ambiguity between causation and temporal meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wording that clearly conveys causal relationships rather than potentially ambiguous temporal language.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'by' preferred over 'per'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'by' rather than 'per' when 'by' is the intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose prepositions that match the intended idiomatic sense in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall standard: pass all 65 checks
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' math paper passes all 65 of Poonen's checks; the list functions as a near-objective rubric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the list collectively as a checklist of stylistic and substantive quality criteria for mathematical writing.
